summary: Specifies the Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol, designed to work with ASAP to meet Reliable Server Pooling requirements. It defines procedures and message formats for a distributed, fault-tolerant registry service that stores and distributes the names of pools and their members. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a shared phone book kept by several clerks. If one clerk goes missing, the others still have the list, so people can still look up which servers are available.

questions: how does enrp maintain pool information
how do enrp servers stay synchronized
what happens when an enrp server fails
subtitle: A distributed, fault-tolerant registry service for server pool membership.

tldr.problem: A centralized registry for server pools becomes a single point of failure. If the registry goes down, clients cannot find servers or learn of pool changes.
tldr.mechanism: ENRP is a distributed registry where multiple ENRP servers maintain identical copies of the pool handlespace. ENRP servers communicate peer-to-peer to share updates, detect failures, and take over a failed peer's data.
tldr.outcome: Pool information remains available even when individual ENRP servers fail. The registry itself scales and becomes resilient.

today: RFC 5353 remains experimental and has not achieved widespread deployment. The ENRP/ASAP protocols are used in research environments and specialized applications requiring high-availability server pooling with distributed fault tolerance.

sections.title: Distributed Handlespace Registry
sections.content:
ENRP (Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol) maintains a distributed registry called the handlespace: a collection of all pool handles and their member servers within an operational scope. Unlike centralized registries, ENRP has no single point of failure. Multiple ENRP servers hold identical copies of the handlespace and synchronize updates peer-to-peer.

ENRP works in conjunction with ASAP. When a pool element (server) wants to register, it contacts ASAP, which forwards the registration to the ENRP server. When a client wants to find servers in a pool, ASAP queries the ENRP server. The ENRP servers themselves are responsible for keeping their copies of the handlespace consistent.
sections.plainLanguage: ENRP is the distributed brain that tracks which servers exist in which pools. It keeps copies on multiple computers so if one breaks, the others keep running.

sections.title: ENRP Message Types
sections.content:
ENRP defines 10 message types for inter-server communication (not for client-server—that is ASAP's job):

ENRP_PRESENCE: Periodic heartbeat sent by each ENRP server to announce it is alive and to probe peer status. Includes a checksum of the sender's pool element data for consistency checking.

ENRP_HANDLE_TABLE_REQUEST/RESPONSE: A starting or synchronizing server asks a peer for a copy of the handlespace data. The response may be split across multiple messages if the handlespace is large.

ENRP_HANDLE_UPDATE: Sent by a server to announce changes to pool memberships—a new pool element registered, an existing one was updated, or one was removed.

ENRP_LIST_REQUEST/RESPONSE: Request the list of known ENRP peers and their connection information.

ENRP_INIT_TAKEOVER/TAKEOVER_SERVER: Used to coordinate takeover when a peer server fails. One server initiates arbitration, others acknowledge, and the designated server takes over the failed server's pool memberships.

ENRP_ERROR: Sent when an unrecognized message or parameter is received.
sections.plainLanguage: ENRP servers say "I'm alive" to each other. They ask "can you send me your list?" to new servers. They tell each other "a server joined" or "a server left". When one dies, they vote on who replaces it.

sections.title: Server Initialization and Peer Discovery
sections.content:
When an ENRP server starts, it first generates a unique 32-bit server ID that persists until reboot. It then goes through a discovery and synchronization phase.

Finding a Mentor Server: The new server must find an existing peer (mentor) that is already in the pool. This can be done through configuration, multicast discovery, or DNS lookup of the ENRP server group.

Acquiring the Peer List: The new server sends ENRP_LIST_REQUEST to the mentor, which responds with a list of all known ENRP servers and their connection information.

Downloading Handlespace Data: The new server sends ENRP_HANDLE_TABLE_REQUEST to the mentor, asking for the full current handlespace. The mentor responds with one or more ENRP_HANDLE_TABLE_RESPONSE messages containing all pool entries.

Once initialized, the server joins the peer-to-peer network, begins receiving heartbeats, and starts sending its own to announce its presence.
sections.plainLanguage: When a new clerk arrives, they ask an existing clerk for the full phone book and the list of other clerks. Then they can start answering questions.

sections.title: Consistency, Updates, and Failure Handling
sections.content:
All ENRP servers maintain identical handlespace data. When a pool element registers, deregisters, or is updated, the ENRP server that received the change broadcasts an ENRP_HANDLE_UPDATE message to all peers, describing the action (add, remove, or modify).

Heartbeat and Peer Monitoring: Each server periodically sends ENRP_PRESENCE messages to peers. A peer is considered dead if its heartbeats stop arriving within a timeout threshold (typically a few minutes). Each ENRP_PRESENCE message also includes a checksum of the sender's pool elements for consistency auditing.

Server Failure and Takeover: When a peer server fails to respond, the other servers detect its absence. To avoid conflict, they run a brief election (ENRP_INIT_TAKEOVER/ACK) to decide which server will take over managing the failed server's pool memberships. The designated server then sends ENRP_TAKEOVER_SERVER to announce that it has assumed responsibility.

Handlespace Auditing: Servers periodically verify consistency by comparing pool element checksums. If a mismatch is found, affected servers request a full or partial re-synchronization of their data.
sections.plainLanguage: Clerks tell each other about changes. If one stops answering, the others vote on who takes over their phone book section. They also double-check that everyone has the same book.

sections.title: Operational Scope and Deployment
sections.content:
ENRP/ASAP operates within a defined operational scope: the set of networks and systems visible to a specific instance of the protocols. The handlespace is flat and local to the operational scope; it is not hierarchical or Internet-wide like DNS.

Pools in different administrative domains can coexist if they have different pool handles. If a client in one domain wants to reach a pool in another, it would use DNS to find that domain's ENRP server group and contact them directly.

An ENRP server channel consists of a list of ENRP server addresses and a well-known port. Servers use this to group-cast messages to all peers (sending multiple copies over separate point-to-point SCTP associations). ASAP clients use a client channel to contact their home ENRP server (a single address and port).
sections.plainLanguage: Each ENRP network operates on its own. They do not talk to each other. You can have one ENRP network in New York and another in Tokyo, but clients in one cannot automatically reach pools in the other.

sections.title: Security Threats and Trust
sections.content:
ENRP deployments face threats including spoofed registrations (an attacker claims a server is in a pool), eavesdropping on pool membership changes, and denial-of-service attacks on the ENRP servers themselves.

The RFC recommends establishing a chain of trust at deployment time. ENRP messages can be authenticated and encrypted using IPsec or SCTP's HMAC-based authentication. ENRP servers should authenticate each other before accepting updates or synchronization requests. Pool elements should be validated before registration is granted.

A secure deployment strategy involves pre-configuring trust relationships (public keys or shared secrets) between ENRP servers and between servers and pool elements. This prevents unauthorized pools from being created and ensures that pool membership changes come from legitimate sources.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad actors could claim servers that do not exist, or read the list of available servers. ENRP servers should authenticate each other and check that registrations come from real servers.
